Cross-checking matters more in August than in June, because a single viral clip in the middle of the holidays can look like demand that will still be there in three weeks. It usually is not.

Sourcing in August, the month the supply chain drags

This is the part that catches people out. August looks like a normal sourcing month from a product page, and it is not. European agents and warehouses run on holiday staffing, and pre-Q4 freight is already filling up as brands ship for the end of the year. The result is quoted delivery times that hold on paper and slip in practice.

Three questions get you a real answer before you spend on ads. Ask when the supplier last shipped this exact variant, not the product family. Ask for the current cut-off time for same-day dispatch, which shortens in August at most warehouses. Ask what happens if the item is out of stock mid-campaign, because a silent substitution on a colour or a capacity turns into a dispute.

For anything with a battery or a liquid, the mosquito lantern, the solar power bank, the after-sun kit, confirm the shipping route and the documentation before the first order rather than after the first customer complaint.

Build the delay into your promise

Add two or three days to whatever the supplier quotes this month and publish that number. A store that promises 12 days and delivers in 10 keeps its reviews. A store that promises 7 and delivers in 12 spends the rest of the season answering tickets, and in a short season that support load is what stops you from scaling.

What kills an August launch

Failed August launches rarely come from a bad product. They come from good products launched with a June mindset.

Treating the calendar as a detail is the first one. Ordering a sample on the 5th, waiting nine days, testing for a week and launching on the 25th means paying full ad prices for a beach product with days of season left. Compress the front of the process or pick a product with autumn runway.

Buying stock on a peak is the second. The temptation in the middle of the month, when a product is finally converting, is to secure inventory. On a strongly seasonal item that is exactly when demand is about to turn, and you end up paying storage until next June.

Selling on the season instead of the situation is the third. Nobody buys a dry bag because it is August. They buy it because they are getting on a boat on Saturday. Every creative should show that Saturday, not the month.

Ignoring the second half of the month is the last one, and the most expensive. Half of August is not summer any more, and the store that swaps its message on the 15th sells to a buyer its competitors stopped talking to.

FAQ

Is August a good month to start dropshipping?

It is a good month to start, and a bad month to be slow. Demand is high, the audience is already buying, and the categories are obvious, so you spend less time guessing. The trade-off is that half the catalogue expires within weeks, which punishes a first-time seller who takes three weeks to get a store live. If you are starting now, pick a product with autumn runway rather than a pure beach item.

How do I know if a product still has time to run?

Look at when the buying reason disappears, not at the trend line. A snorkel mask stops making sense when the sea is cold, a solar light does not. Then subtract your delivery time and your test period from the weeks left. If the result is under two weeks of actual selling, the product is a next-year candidate.

What do I do with stock that doesn't sell before September?

Nothing dramatic. Storing a light, non-perishable seasonal item until next spring usually costs less than discounting it into a market that has moved on, and a deep clearance in September teaches your audience to wait for the next markdown. The exception is anything with a battery, where holding stock for months brings its own risks.

Do I have to change my whole catalogue at the end of the month?

No, and doing it is a common mistake. Keep the products that carry into autumn, retire the pure summer ones, and change the situation shown in your creatives for everything in between. A full catalogue swap throws away the product pages, reviews and pixel data you just spent a month building.

Do delivery times really change in August?

Yes, in both directions. Warehouse staffing drops with holidays while pre-Q4 freight starts competing for space, so quoted times hold less well than in spring. Add two or three days to the supplier's estimate before you publish a delivery promise, and check the cut-off time for same-day dispatch, which often moves earlier this month.

Which of these products keep selling in autumn?

The after-sun repair kit, the solar string lights, the cooler backpack and the filter bottle. Repair beauty runs while the damage is still visible, lighting picks up as evenings shorten, and both the backpack and the bottle move from beach use to school and commute use without a new product page.

Is it too late to launch travel gear mid-August?

Not for the products that survive the trip. Filter bottles, dry bags and cooler backpacks keep selling to hikers, commuters and school runs well past the holidays. Pure holiday items like snorkel masks are a different story, and after the 20th they are better held for next season than pushed with paid traffic.

Should I start preparing Q4 now?

Yes, quietly and in parallel. August is when you can still test suppliers, creatives and store structure without the ad costs of November. Use the month to validate what works, then rotate into seasonal Q4 products with a store that is already proven rather than one you built in a hurry in October.

Where do I find suppliers for these products?

AliExpress and CJdropshipping cover most of the list in 7 to 12 days. In August the choice of supplier matters more than the platform: order the sample first, confirm the folded dimensions and the packaging, and ask about the shipping route for anything carrying a battery or a liquid. A supplier that answers quickly in August is worth more than one that is two euros cheaper.

Do I need a product research tool?

You can do it manually with the Facebook ad library, marketplace best-sellers and a spreadsheet, and in a slow month that is fine. In a month where the window is measured in weeks, a product research tool like Copyfy or AutoDS mostly buys you time, by showing performance data, competitor ads and saturation in one place. The six gates and a real sample still decide what you launch.

Your first week, day by day

A launch that starts on the 1st and a launch that starts on the 20th are not the same job. This sequence assumes you start today and want ads running within a week.

  • Days 1 and 2: pick two products from the list that share one theme, and check the remaining runway of each before anything else.
  • Day 2: order samples and, in the same message, ask the supplier the three sourcing questions above.
  • Days 3 and 4: build one landing page per product with an honest delivery estimate, and film the demo around a real situation rather than a studio shot.
  • Day 5: launch three creatives per product on a small equal budget.
  • Day 7: read the data, kill what is flat, and put everything behind the one that moved.
  • Week 2: reorder on the winner only, and start rewriting its creative for the second half of the month.

The sample often arrives after the ads are already running, and that is acceptable in a short season as long as you have not scaled yet. What is not acceptable is scaling on a product you have never held.

Start before the window closes

Pick two products that fit one theme, score their remaining runway, and get a test live this week rather than next. August rewards the seller who moves first and punishes the one who waits for a perfect setup, because the demand does not wait for either. Set up tracking before you touch anything

Connect Google Search Console and Google Analytics 4 on day one. Without that baseline you cannot prove any optimization worked. Shopify has a native GA4 channel in the admin, which takes about 20 minutes to connect.

Then set your primary domain under Settings > Domains so every version of your store resolves to one address.

Fix titles, meta descriptions and H1s

Title tags carry more weight than any other on-page element you can edit in five minutes. Write them to earn the click in the SERP, not to please a robot.

The pattern that works on ecommerce SERPs:

Primary keyword + qualifier + brand in 55 to 60 characters.

Example: Waterproof Running Headphones IPX7 | 12h Battery | Brand

Meta descriptions are not a ranking factor. They do shift click-through rate, which is why they earn an hour of your time. Include the keyword, one differentiator and one reason to click.

Missing meta descriptions let Google create its own snippet from your page text. That snippet is rarely the sentence you would have picked.

Ensure each template renders exactly one H1. Some themes wrap the logo in an H1 on every page, which dilutes the signal across the store.

Image optimization the fast way

Rename image files before upload. waterproof-running-headphones-black.webp beats IMG_4471.jpg in Google Images, where a real share of product discovery happens.

Then write descriptive alt text for someone who cannot see the image. No keyword stuffing. One accurate sentence per image, naming the product and its key visual detail.

Compress every image to WebP, aim for under 100 KB per visual, and let the Shopify CDN handle delivery. Oversized images are the most common reason a Shopify product page fails its LCP target.

How to submit your sitemap to Google Search Console

Shopify generates your XML sitemap automatically at yourstore.com/sitemap.xml. You cannot edit that file. It acts as an index pointing to child files: products, collections, blogs and pages.

To submit your sitemap:

  1. Open Search Console and select your domain property.
  2. Click Sitemaps in the left menu.
  3. Type sitemap.xml in the field and submit.
  4. Come back after 48 hours to check for read errors.

Ensure the property you pick matches the domain customers actually see, otherwise the report stays empty.

This is the least glamorous SEO task on the list. Skipping it costs weeks of indexing on a new store.

One detail people miss: if a product is unpublished from the Online Store sales channel but still active elsewhere, it can linger in the sitemap. Check the Pages report in Search Console monthly for URLs that should no longer be there.

A product page ranks when it answers the query better than the SERP result above it. On ecommerce queries that means specifications, real customer reviews, shipping facts and photos taken from angles your competitors skipped.

Keep the handle short. /products/waterproof-running-headphones beats a 12-word slug carrying supplier codes. Three or four words is enough, with the main term first.

  • Three to five specification bullets with numbers
  • A short paragraph on use case and fit
  • Shipping, returns and how to reach customer service

That structure covers long-tail terms naturally. You end up ranking for queries you never targeted, because real customers search in specifics: a size, a material, a use case.

BigSpy features in detail

Ad search and filtering

Search runs on keywords, then narrows through filters:

  • Platform and country
  • Ad format and industry
  • Call to action and date range
  • Engagement counts

Sorting covers last seen, created time, likes, comments, shares and duration. No demographics filter, so gender and age targeting stay hidden.

The exclusion filter is the one most users miss. Dropping unwanted terms into the exclude field reduces the duplicate creative issue that shows up repeatedly in negative reviews.

Audience data is the visible gap. BigSpy surfaces the creative and the advertiser but exposes no targeting parameters, so you cannot reverse-engineer who a campaign was built for. Premium Meta-focused solutions like AdSpy and Anstrex do expose that layer.

Work around it by reading the creative. The audience is usually written into the hook, the on-screen text and the comment section.

One mechanic changes how you use the tool. BigSpy documentation states that each search, filter, sort or page counts as one query. Paginating five pages costs five queries, not one.

That reframes every plan limit on the pricing page: 20 daily queries is not 20 research sessions. Set your keyword first, then filters, then sort. Reverse that order and a single topic burns a third of your quota.

Video creatives, hooks and ad formats

BigSpy indexes static images, video and playable ad types across its ten networks. Video is where the useful signal sits for ecommerce sellers, especially anything viral.

Combine three filters: video format, ad duration above 30 days and a recent date range. Video that ran long over the last three to six months is the clearest sign a creative found its audience and is paying for itself, the closest thing to a profitability proxy this type of tool offers. A creative that ran for months two years ago proves nothing today.

Then harvest hooks. Pull the first three seconds of twenty running video ads in your niche and you own a hook bank worth more than any swipe file of finished creatives. Hooks transfer across products and categories. Full videos rarely do.

Creative inspiration and the swipe file

Saved filters and folders make BigSpy usable long term. Configure a searchable query once, name it, reload it in one click.

Downloads work on a separate daily counter from queries. Each creative you pull counts once. The quota resets the next day with no rollover, so downloading in batches beats saving one at a time.

BigSpy also runs curated feeds with weekly updates. Top Charts ranks advertisements by estimated impressions, New Trending surfaces fresh creatives and the trends emerging across industries. Top Charts sits behind the VIP Enterprise tier, which restricts its value for most readers of this review.

The Chrome extension covers the other half of the workflow. Once installed, ad intelligence surfaces while you browse instead of sending you back to the dashboard each time something catches your eye. It pairs with saved filters for repeat sessions.

Store spy capabilities

The weakest area relative to what dropshippers expect from this type of tool.

BigSpy offers page analysis for Facebook, Google and TikTok, plus a domain analysis module and a TikTok Shop section for shopping data. Click from an ad to the advertiser profile and you see their active ad count and historical creative output.

What you do not get is Shopify store analytics: visitor estimates, revenue modelling, bestseller ranking or theme detection. No landing page URLs collected, no export to CSV, no integration for teams wanting automation.

If your workflow depends on validating that a competitor store actually converts, BigSpy is not the tool that answers it.

Interface, dashboard and learning curve

The dashboard is functional rather than modern. Ads display in a visual grid, filters sit in a left rail, saved searches live in folders at the top. Nothing you have not seen before, nothing that gets in the way either.

Capterra reviewers score ease of use 4.7 and call the layout intuitive. Trustpilot runs the other way: pages that load slowly and a feed that feels cluttered once several networks unlock at once.

Both readings hold. Navigation is straightforward when you know which competitor to monitor, harder when you browse without criteria, because nothing in the interface helps you refine a broad market into a shortlist.

Onboarding is thin: tutorials and a blog, no guided setup. Budget an hour of practice before it feels efficient.

Performance signals and AI

BigSpy leans on two proprietary metrics rather than an AI layer. No AI-powered creative analysis, no automated scoring.

Popularity combines an ad's duration, how often the system rediscovers it and its measured marketing effect. Impression is an algorithmic estimate of exposure that BigSpy states is not equal to view count.

Both are proxy signals. Engagement correlates loosely with profitability, never reliably. Use ad duration as your primary filter: a campaign still running after 30 days spends real money to stay live, a more precise indicator than a like count.

BigSpy claims 100,000 ads added hourly. Capterra reviewers, who rate it 4.8 out of 5 overall, flag refresh lag as their most common complaint: current competitor ads occasionally arrive delayed or slightly outdated.

For creative inspiration that lag is irrelevant. For catching a trending product while the campaign is still scaling, it matters. Time-sensitive insights are not this platform's strength, so plan your testing around it.

1. Pet accessories

Pet owners buy on guilt and love. Neither emotion price-shops.

Slow-feeder bowls, grooming gloves and anti-pull leads fix a problem the owner complains about out loud, which makes the video ad write itself.

The category repeats. A buyer who trusts you on a lead comes back for food toppers, toys and a travel kit, so lifetime value climbs without new ad spend.

2. Skincare tools and targeted care

Skincare items are high margin products because the buyer pays for a result, not for materials. A gua sha tool costs under $4 landed and retails above $29 when the offer speaks to one concern.

Skip generic beauty. Target one problem, one skin type, one age group.

People search for solutions rather than categories, so "jawline sculpting for oily skin" outperforms "beauty tool" on every metric that matters.

  • Check before launch: claims compliance in your market, before you write a single ad.
  • Watch out for saturation on viral items. Look for the sub-niche two steps behind the trend.

3. Phone accessories and chargers

Buyers replace them yearly and never compare specs seriously. Magnetic chargers, camera lens protectors and car mounts land under $6 and sell above $19.

For a first-time seller, this is the safest entry on the list. Cheap SKU, easy demo, few returns.

Volume covers the small ticket. Bundle two items to lift the average order value from $22 to $38 without extra ad spend, the fastest profit fix on this list.

Tech accessories are light, so shipping stays cheap on every route. Gaming accessories follow the same pattern with a slightly older buyer and a higher ticket.

  • Check before launch: device compatibility per model. One wrong SKU generates a wave of support tickets.
  • Watch out for the price war on cables. Sell the mount, not the commodity.

4. Home fitness equipment

Resistance bands, ab rollers and adjustable dumbbells peak twice a year, in January and before summer. The home gym crowd fills the gap in between.

Health and wellness products carry high perceived value when you attach a program. A $12 band set with a printable 30 day plan retails at $39 and returns less than a bare band.

The buyer who finishes the program comes back for the next kit.

  • Check before launch: shipping weight above 2 kg kills the margin. Ask for the boxed weight, not the item weight.
  • Watch out for quality. Snapped bands generate refunds and bad reviews fast.

5. Kitchen gadgets

The most demo-friendly items on this list. A 10 second clip of a garlic press doing its job converts colder audiences than any copy you could write.

They gift well too, which stacks a Q4 spike on top of steady demand.

Bundle two or three related tools in one box and you defend a $39 price point that a single gadget could not hold. Gift boxes with a printed recipe card sell at a premium in December.

  • Check before launch: search the product name plus "review" to see the complaints buyers already have.
  • Watch out for electrical certification if the item plugs in.

6. Home office furniture and desk gear

Remote work turned desk setups into a hobby. Monitor risers and cable organizers sell to people who redecorate their workspace the way others redecorate a living room.

Small furniture and storage perform best with a professional buyer who expenses the purchase. Ticket size and repeat rate both climb.

A $14 landed desk shelf retails at $49 because it reads as furniture, not as an accessory. Buyers rarely compare it to anything.

  • Check before launch: dimensions in inches and centimeters. Wrong fit is the top return reason here.
  • Watch out for bulky shipping. Flat-pack designs protect your profit.

7. Smart home devices

Smart plugs, motion sensors and WiFi bulbs are one-problem solutions. The buyer wants that problem gone.

Profitability sits lower here than elsewhere on the list. Average order value repairs it, so sell the system rather than the single device.

A three-sensor kit at $79 beats one unit at $29 on every profit line. The setup guide you write becomes your differentiator.

  • Check before launch: app support and firmware updates from the supplier. A device built around a dead app becomes a support problem.
  • Watch out for compatibility claims. Alexa and Google Home support must be verified, never assumed.

8. Personalized jewelry

The highest physical margin on this list. A name necklace costs $4 to produce and sells at $49 because the piece is unique and no buyer can compare it to anything.

Gifting drives the calendar: birthdays, anniversaries, Mother's Day. Each one hands you a peak that needs no discount.

Custom work also removes returns, since personalization counts as final sale in most policies. The trade-off is production time, so set delivery expectations on the product page and in the confirmation email.

  • Check before launch: your partner's turnaround time in peak season. December doubles it.
  • Watch out for spelling errors. One character wrong equals a full remake at your cost.

9. Print on demand apparel

A t-shirt business starts with zero stock, which is why so many first-time sellers begin here. Printify and Printful handle the printing and the fulfillment. You handle the design and the marketing.

Margins are the thinnest on this list. A t-shirt costs $9 to $12 through a print partner and sells at $28 to $34, so 55 to 65% before ads. Hoodies improve the math with a $24 base and a $59 retail price.

You price the design, not the shirt. A generic shirt competes on price with Amazon and loses. A shirt that speaks to one identity, one job or one inside joke sells at full price and travels through organic social.

Where you sell it changes the math too.

On Etsy, a personalized or handmade shirt reaches shoppers already searching, in exchange for listing fees and a marketplace that keeps the customer. On your own store, traffic costs more and the buyer stays yours.

Test one design per niche before you print a catalogue. Ten shirt ideas at $20 of ads each tell you which one deserves a brand.

  • Check before launch: order a sample from Printify or any partner you shortlist. Print quality on the same file varies between suppliers.
  • Watch out for athleisure. Fit complaints run higher than on classic shirts and hoodies.

10. Wall art and home decor

Saturation stays low because most sellers avoid fragile-looking items. Framed prints, canvas sets and peel-and-stick murals ship flat and arrive intact when the packaging is right.

Style decides the sale here more than the tag, which makes visual ads mandatory. A room render outperforms a product-on-white photo every time.

Eco-friendly framing and recycled paper stock justify a higher price with this audience.

  • Check before launch: breakage rate with your supplier. Ask for the packaging spec in writing.
  • Watch out for licensed artwork. Only sell designs you own or license properly.

11. Baby and toddler gear

New parents buy fast, buy often, and read every review before they do. Safety-driven items like bath thermometers, sleep aids and silicone feeding sets carry strong margins, then repeat naturally as the child grows.

Trust converts this category. Certifications, material details and real photos do more than a promo code. One honest review with a photo outperforms any discount you could run.

  • Check before launch: safety standards in your market. This category is regulated.
  • Watch out for toys with small parts. Compliance paperwork is not optional.

12. Outdoor and camping gear

Seasonal demand with a long tail. Portable solar chargers, compact stoves and hammocks reach a buyer who spends on gear without blinking.

Seasonality is a feature once you plan it. Launch in early spring, scale through summer, then move budget to the gifting categories in Q4 instead of fighting a dead auction.

  • Check before launch: last year's trend curve on Google Trends, to time your entry six weeks early.
  • Watch out for weight. Anything above 3 kg needs a higher ticket to stay profitable.

Gross margin = (selling price minus landed cost) divided by selling price

Landed cost means the product plus shipping plus customs plus payment processing on the purchase. A seller who forgets those three lines discovers the real margin after the first hundred orders.

Revenue on its own means little. A store at $50,000 of revenue with a 12% margin earns less than one at $20,000 with 30%. A consistent 30% across 12 months beats one lucky product at 60%.

Finding a product takes an afternoon. Validating it takes 30 minutes and saves the $500 you would have burned learning the same lesson from ads.

Step 1: confirm the demand is live, not historical

Step 2: read the competition through their ads

Open an ad library or a spy tool and pull every live ad on the product. Three things matter:

Ask three suppliers for a quote at 50, 200 and 500 units, with boxed weight included. Order a sample from the two best. Handling the item tells you in five minutes what a spec sheet never will, and the photos you shoot become your first creative.

A second source protects you later. When one factory raises prices in peak season, the seller with a backup supplier keeps the profit.

Check expected delivery time to your main market. Anything past 12 days needs either a local warehouse or a very clear promise on the product page.

Budget $100 to $300 per product over five to seven days. Two or three creatives, one audience, no fancy setup. The goal is a clean read on whether the offer reaches a buyer at an acceptable cost.

Five mistakes that turn profitable products into losses

Launching from a listicle alone

Any published list is a snapshot. By the time it ranks on Google, the auction has changed. Check live ads before you trust any list, including this one.

Confusing viral with profitable

A product with 2 million TikTok views and a 45% margin loses money at scale. Views are not sales. Sales at a thin margin are not profit.

Ignoring the fully landed cost

A seller prices against the supplier's unit price and forgets shipping, customs and processing fees. That habit turns a planned 70% margin into a real 48%. Most failing ecommerce businesses lose money on this line.

Testing ten products at once

Split budget produces ten inconclusive tests. Two products with $100 each teach you more than ten with $20. Pick one target audience per test so the data means something.

Quitting a winner too early

A product that breaks even on day five with a rising add-to-cart rate is often one creative away from working. Cut the losers fast, give the borderline cases one honest retest.

FAQ

What is a good profit margin for online products?

Aim for 65 to 75% gross margin on physical goods. That range leaves room for a 2.5 ROAS on ads, payment fees and a normal return rate, while keeping an expected 15 to 30% net profit for the seller.

Digital products sit above 90% gross margin. Acquisition runs slower because trust takes longer to build.

How do I know if a product is too saturated?

Count the live ads. Above 50 active campaigns with visible price cuts in the creatives, you are entering a price war rather than a market.

Two other signals: the same creative reused by five sellers, plus Amazon listings with thousands of reviews at a price you cannot beat. When both appear, the trend has moved on, so look one sub-niche deeper.

Which platform should I choose to sell online?

Your own store if you plan to run ads. Shopify plus a light app stack gives you control over the offer, the pricing and the customer experience, which is where the profit lives. A video demo and a strong angle carry the sale there.

Marketplaces are the other option. Amazon and Etsy include the traffic and the trust, then take a cut plus your customer data. Each e-commerce platform charges differently.

Selling the same product on both works, provided you recalculate the numbers per channel, since Amazon fees alone move the math by 20 points.

How often should I refresh my product research?

Weekly for active tests, monthly for your category watch. Niches grow and saturate in weeks, so a product validated this month can be crowded by the next.

Set a recurring 30 minute block, pull the live ads in your niche, note what is new and what disappeared.

What are the easiest things to sell online without stock?

A t-shirt store, digital downloads and dropshipped accessories. All three let you start with no inventory, so the cheapest option carries only your ad test as a real cost.

Beginner-friendly rarely means profitable. These categories stay crowded because entry is simple, which puts the work back on your angle and your creative.

Are digital products more profitable than physical products?

Per sale, yes. A $49 course with no cost of goods beats a $49 product with a $12 landed cost on every profit line.

Per month of work, it depends. Physical items borrow demand that already exists. Digital products require you to create the demand first, and that takes an audience most sellers do not have yet.

What is the most accurate Shopify app detector?

None wins everywhere. Instant is strong because it reports confidence per app. Running two detectors and comparing the overlap gives a more accurate picture than trusting one.

Can store owners see that you scanned their store?

No. You access the same public pages a shopper does. Detectors and extensions read them the way any visitor's browser does. Nothing shows up in the merchant's analytics as a scan.

Can I detect apps on a password-protected store?

No. If the store is locked behind a password, the page source is not public, so there is nothing to inspect.

What is the difference between an app detector and a theme detector?

An app detector lists installed apps. A theme detector identifies a Shopify store’s theme and often its version. Most tools return both from a single URL.

Are browser extensions better than online tools?

For volume, yes. For one check, a web tool wins because there is nothing to install. The extension also keeps a history of the stores you checked, which a web tool rarely does.

Can I see the apps in a store's checkout?

Only by reaching the checkout yourself. Add an item to the cart, start the process, then inspect that page. Automated tools stop at the storefront.

How accurate is app detection?

Front-end apps: reliable. Apps integrated into the theme by a developer: often missed. Back-office apps: never.

Native Shopify integrations get counted by some tools and ignored by others. Databases receive their updates on their own schedule, so a recent install can lag. Treat the output as a strong signal, not a comprehensive inventory.

Shopify Admin, then Apps and sales channels. You get every app installed on your store plus billing, which no external tool can access.

Can I detect apps on any ecommerce platform?

Wappalyzer and BuiltWith work on any ecommerce platform. Shopify specific detectors only return useful data on Shopify.

Why bother knowing a competitor's apps?

It shortcuts your testing. In e-commerce that is the expensive part. Instead of paying to discover which review or bundle tool converts in your market, you build from a list that already survived one.

Introduction: Exporting a CSV to paste into a chat that knows nothing about your store is over. Four ways to connect, and the one that actually fits your profile.
Article:
Key takeaways:

  • The Shopify app for Claude installs in three screens, with no code at all.
  • The Shopify AI Toolkit runs through the CLI and opens access to the API schemas.
  • Only one store stays connected at a time on your Claude account.
  • You stay responsible for every action Claude runs inside your admin.
  • The workflows that pay off: product pages, customer reviews, performance reports.

You spend your evenings exporting Shopify data to paste into an AI chat that knows nothing about your store. The result: generic answers. The Shopify app for Claude removes that back and forth. This guide covers the four connection methods and what they actually change.

Create your store for free with AI in 5 minutes!

The 4 methods to connect Claude to Shopify

MethodWho it is forAuthenticationTechnical levelBest use case
MCP Desktop (Shopify app for Claude)Merchant, dropshipper, agencyShopify OAuthNoneDay-to-day store management
Shopify AI Toolkit (CLI plugin)Developer, power userNone, except for store managementMediumAPI docs, code validation, migration
Dev MCP server (npx)DeveloperNoneHighCursor, VS Code, Codex
CSV copilotBeginnerNoneZeroOne-off analysis with no install

If you want to run your store in plain language, go with method 1. If you code your theme or your extensions, go with method 2. Nothing stops you from installing both: they sit side by side on the same machine without conflict.

The Shopify apps built for AI tools are not published on the Shopify App Store. You install them straight from the AI tool.

Method 1: MCP Desktop, the Shopify app for Claude

The app is built by Shopify. It works on Claude web, the Desktop app, the mobile app, Claude Code and the API. Budget under five minutes for the whole setup.

Step 1: open the connector directory

In the Claude interface, open Customize then Connectors. Search for Shopify in the directory, then start the connection. The same screen exists on Claude Desktop and on mobile.

Two configuration details worth knowing:

  • Connectors are only active inside private projects
  • A conversation holding synced data cannot be shared

On a Team plan, a Request button sometimes replaces the connect action. Your administrator then approves the connector at the organization level.

Step 2: authorize access from your Shopify admin

Claude redirects you to the Shopify admin for OAuth authentication. The process asks for three separate confirmations, each on its own screen.

You authorize the app, you approve the data access level, then the tool can interact with your store.

Two safeguards apply at the same time:

  • The access you grant to the app
  • Your own user permissions in the admin

A staff account that can read products without editing them cannot hand that write permission to Claude.

One good thing about the OAuth flow: there is no token to copy or store. Shopify handles the exchange, unlike a third-party MCP server that often asks you for a plain-text access token in a configuration file.

Step 3: choose between read-only and write access

Read this screen before you click. You cannot narrow the access scope after approval without uninstalling the app entirely.

In read-only mode, Claude reads your orders, your products and your stats without touching anything. With write access, it can create products, change prices and generate discount codes.

Our recommendation for a first setup: stay in read-only for two weeks. You can switch on write access once you know which requests you run day to day. This gradual setup keeps nasty surprises away from a live catalog.

If the app later asks for a higher level, you get a fresh authorization prompt. To revoke the access token, uninstall the app or the connector from your admin settings.

Step 4: check that the connection works

Run this verification request. It tests reads on orders, products and analytics in one go.

Prompt to copy
List my 10 best-selling products over the last 30 days, with revenue, order count and remaining stock per variant.

If Claude sends back a table with your real numbers, your setup is good. If it asks you for an export, the connection is not live. Also check that it is querying the right store before you go further.

Step 5: switch stores when you manage several

Only one store stays connected at a time, even when your stores belong to the same Shopify organization.

To switch, just ask Claude to connect to another store. It disconnects the first one then starts a new authorization. Budget thirty seconds per switch.

For an agency juggling ten client accounts, this is the most annoying limit of the current system. Plan work sessions per store rather than constant switching.

Method 2: the Shopify AI Toolkit on the command line

The Shopify AI Toolkit is the official way to connect an AI agent to the Shopify developer ecosystem. It does not replace the app described above: it covers a different need.

What is the Shopify AI Toolkit?

It is Shopify’s official tool for plugging an AI agent into the documentation, the GraphQL schemas, Liquid validation and the Polaris components. The repository has 530 stars on GitHub. The difference with the method 1 connector: it runs locally and asks for no authentication on the development side.

What the Toolkit adds on top

  • Search across the Shopify documentation and the API schemas without leaving your editor
  • Validation of GraphQL queries, Liquid templates and theme extensions
  • Store management through the store execute capabilities of the Shopify CLI
  • Automatic updates as soon as Shopify adds new capabilities

The use case that pays off most is extension migration. Checkout and customer account extensions on an API version earlier than 2025-10 have to move to Polaris web components. The Toolkit automates most of that repetitive work by following the official migration guide.

The install commands for each tool

ToolCommand
Claude Codeclaude plugin install shopify-ai-toolkit@claude-plugins-official
Codexcodex plugin add shopify@openai-curated
Cursor/add-plugin shopify in the chat
Antigravity CLIagy plugin install https://github.com/Shopify/shopify-ai-toolkit
VS CodeCommand Palette then Chat: Install Plugin From Source
Skills onlynpx skills add Shopify/shopify-ai-toolkit

Prerequisite: Node.js 18 or higher. To install a single capability, add the skill flag. Example with the GraphQL Admin API:

Command
npx skills add Shopify/shopify-ai-toolkit --skill shopify-admin

Skills added by hand do not update on their own. You pull new versions manually. Other option: install the full plugin to skip that maintenance.

Telemetry is on by default

The Toolkit scripts send a usage event to Shopify on every call. The payload includes:

  • The name of the tool, the skill and the model
  • The text of your search query
  • The validated code
  • Your last message in Claude Code, truncated to 2,000 characters, base64 encoded

Three ways to cut the collection, all equivalent. The one Shopify recommends is an empty file, on macOS and Linux:

Command
mkdir -p ~/.config/shopify-ai-toolkit && touch ~/.config/shopify-ai-toolkit/opt-out

On Windows the same file goes to %APPDATA%\shopify-ai-toolkit\opt-out. Otherwise, an environment variable is enough:

Command
OPT_OUT_INSTRUMENTATION=true
DO_NOT_TRACK=1

Once any of the three is in place, nothing turns the collection back on.

Method 3: the Dev MCP server, without the plugin

The Dev server runs locally and asks for no authentication.

Command
claude mcp add --transport stdio shopify-dev-mcp -- npx -y @shopify/dev-mcp@latest

Restart Claude Code after adding it, otherwise the configuration never loads. On Cursor, VS Code or Codex, you can add the same server through a JSON or TOML configuration file.

Method 4: the CSV copilot mode, zero install

You do not have admin rights on your client’s store. Or you just want to test before you authorize anything.

The idea: you export your products, your orders or your customers as CSV from the Shopify admin, then you drop the files into a Claude project.

It works well for a one-off analysis. It does not work for taking action. Claude cannot change anything in your store and your data stays frozen at export time.

Use this mode for a monthly catalog audit or a cohort analysis. Move to the app as soon as you repeat the same request every week.

Going further: third-party MCP servers

Two limits of the official app push some merchants to add a third-party server, which is available on the Shopify App Store.

The first one is permission granularity. Apps like ShopMCP let you create a dedicated MCP endpoint with:

  • Per-resource permissions
  • An audit log per connection
  • An automatic backup of theme files before every change

The second one is analytics performance. The official app and most community servers query the GraphQL Admin API.

Perfect for store operations, slow as soon as you cross tens of thousands of orders. Tools like Mipler query a pre-synced database for cohort and customer lifetime value analysis.

What the connection changes in practice

Without the integration, you describe your store to an artificial intelligence that has never seen it. With it, the model queries your data live. Three differences show up in the first week.

You get numbers on your catalog without preparing an export. You ask in plain language, Claude goes and looks in the admin.

You move from analysis to action. A connected tool can create a product, adjust stock or generate a discount code. A CSV file stops at the diagnosis.

You claw back time on repetitive work. Product pages, weekly reports and customer support triage: those are the tasks where automation pays off fastest.

Who gets the most out of it:

  • The solo dropshipper who writes their own product pages
  • The agency running several client stores
  • The ecommerce merchant who wants a dashboard without opening ten tabs

8 dropshipping workflows with Claude and Shopify

Every prompt in this section is ready to copy. Adjust the numbers to your own business.

Workflow 1: split your winners from your dead products

Prompt to copy
Analyze my sales over the last 60 days. Sort my products into three groups: scale, optimize, cut. For each product, give revenue, order count, return rate and remaining stock.

Claude sees what sells in your store. It does not see what sells everywhere else. That is where Copyfy takes over: it goes and finds the items taking off on competing stores and inside live ads.

Workflow 2: generate your product pages in bulk

Prompt to copy
Write the product pages for the items in my New arrivals collection. For each product: a title of 60 characters max, a meta description of 155 characters, 5 benefit bullets and a 120-word paragraph. Direct tone, second person.

On a catalog of fifty items, you go from two days of writing to about thirty minutes of proofreading. Remember to check the generated content before you publish.

Workflow 3: pull your marketing angles out of customer reviews

Prompt to copy
Analyze every review on my 5 best-selling products. Pull out the 10 benefits customers mention on their own, the 5 recurring objections and the exact wording I can reuse in my ads.

This is the most underused workflow. Your customers write your ad hooks for you.

Workflow 4: audit your store SEO

Prompt to copy
Review my 30 most visited product pages. Flag duplicate titles, missing or overly long meta descriptions, images with no alt text and pages under 200 words.

A manual SEO audit on thirty pages takes half a day. Here you get the prioritized list in one request.

Workflow 5: triage your customer support

Prompt to copy
Summarize customer requests from the last 7 days by category: shipping, faulty product, refund, pre-purchase question. Give the volume per category and draft a template reply for the three most frequent ones.

The triage takes a few seconds and produces three reusable template replies. The rest of your inbox turns into a queue of exceptions instead of a wall.

Workflow 6: launch a promo and adjust your stock

Prompt to copy
Create a BLACK20 discount code at 20% on my Winter collection, valid from 25 to 30 November, limited to one use per customer. First check that stock covers three times last month’s sales on that collection.

This request needs write access. Claude shows you the action before it creates the discount code.

Workflow 7: your weekly performance report

Prompt to copy
Every Monday, build my custom dashboard for the week: revenue, average order value, conversion rate, top 5 products, comparison with the previous week and the three anomalies that deserve action.

A self-running report you read in two minutes replaces the half hour spent inside Shopify analytics. Keep a benchmark in mind when you read the conversion line: the industry standard sits between 2 and 3 %.

Workflow 8: prepare your competitive analysis

Prompt to copy
Starting from my 10 most profitable products, list the criteria that set them apart: price range, positioning, main promise. Then write the 5 questions to ask about a competing store to compare it with mine.

Claude builds the framework. It does not fill it in: the data on competing stores and their running ads is not in your admin. Copyfy fills the cells.

Which automation strategy fits your stage

Not every merchant needs the same setup. The volumes below are a marker, not a threshold: what actually decides is the time you spend on repetitive tasks and your ability to spot a wrong answer.

Feed video ads: start with portrait

In Feed, your ad appears among posts from followed accounts, groups and Pages. Make the product and its benefit clear quickly.

Export settings to limit quality loss

Compression can erase fine detail, especially if the source file is already degraded. Provide a good-quality source, then inspect the video after uploading.

  • Suggested container: MP4 with H.264 video and AAC audio.
  • Square pixels, fixed frame rate and progressive scan, following Meta’s recommendations.
  • Stereo AAC audio at 128 kbps or higher for placements that recommend it.
  • Resolution: match the canvas to the placement recommendation and your source quality.
  • Bitrate: adjust for motion and detail, then check the uploaded result.
  • Frame rate: keep motion smooth without unnecessarily converting the source.

Moving from 30 to 60 fps does not automatically double file size. At the same duration and total bitrate, file size stays similar. A higher frame rate may need more bitrate to preserve detail.

Quality does not depend on one universal bitrate threshold. Artificially increasing a blurry source’s resolution cannot recreate detail; start with the best file available.

To avoid double compression, always export from the original project. Exporting an already compressed video again compounds defects with each generation.

6 mistakes that can waste your ad budget

Using the same dimensions everywhere can cause bars or cropping. A square and a full-screen vertical video provide different spaces for your composition.

Ignoring safe zones can hide your CTA or captions. Check the preview with the caption and button you will actually use.

Reducing bitrate too far can degrade detail. For example, 15 seconds at 12 Mbps equals roughly 22.5 MB of video, excluding audio and container overhead. That bitrate is an example, not a Meta requirement.

Accepting automatic edits without reviewing them can change your framing. Turn off only those that make your ad’s presentation worse.

Leaving out captions means viewers watching without sound miss part of the message. CapCut can generate captions automatically; review names, prices and transcription errors.

Checking only one screen can leave readability problems unnoticed. Review the result on several devices where possible.

Check the preview on Android and iPhone before publishing.

The limit depends on placement: up to 241 minutes in Feed, 3 minutes in Facebook Stories and no maximum listed in the Facebook Reels specification. Other placements and objectives may impose their own limits.

The Meta specifications reviewed accept MP4, MOV and GIF. For video with sound, MP4 with H.264 and AAC audio is a practical choice. An accepted extension does not remove the need to meet the other requirements.

An already compressed source or a bitrate too low for the scene’s detail may lose sharpness during processing. Export from the original project, keep your chosen ratio and compare the local file with the uploaded preview.

What a useful course should cover

A dropshipping SEO course should connect Google visibility with the constraints of a real store: margin, catalog, suppliers and customer experience.

Can you learn dropshipping SEO for free?

Yes. Shopify Academy, Google documentation, Ahrefs and experienced creators cover the foundations. The hidden cost is selection. Set aside several dozen hours to learn, practise and check whether advice is still current.

  • Start with keywords and search intent

The four SEO levers of an online store

1. Structure

Create one useful category per commercial intent, not one category per item. Keep URLs, variants and filters controlled so they do not produce hundreds of weak pages.

2. Internal links

Connect each product with its category and the guides that answer pre-purchase questions. Clear internal paths help shoppers and search engines.

3. Content

Comparisons, buying guides and problem-solving articles capture research demand. Each piece should lead naturally to the relevant commercial page.

4. Authority

Links from credible, relevant sites strengthen important pages. Judge editorial fit, real traffic and link placement before counting domains.

How long does organic traffic take?

Early signals can appear within a few months, but stable traffic often takes longer. Competition, domain history, catalog size and links all change the timeline.

Is Shopify or WooCommerce better for dropshipping SEO?

Both can rank. WooCommerce offers more technical control; Shopify reduces maintenance. Choose the platform you can operate cleanly for years.

Does a course replace a product research tool?

No. A course teaches a method; a tool supplies recent market data. Neither replaces demand, margin and supplier validation.

Is dropshipping SEO still viable?

You can scale a campaign at 2x ROAS and still lose money. The gap between the number in your ad account and the money your store keeps starts with break-even ROAS. Calculate yours in two minutes.

What break-even ROAS is and why it is a floor

Break-even ROAS is the minimum return on ad spend required to cover the variable costs attached to a sale. Below it, each attributed order destroys contribution profit. Above it, the order starts contributing to fixed overhead and profit.

BEROAS means break-even return on ad spend. It answers one practical question: how much revenue must each advertising dollar generate before the order stops losing money?

Treat it as a floor, not a target. A campaign sitting exactly at break-even pays the supplier, fulfilment and transaction costs but leaves nothing for overhead or owner profit.

Break-even ROAS vs target ROAS

MetricWhat it measuresHow to set it
Break-even ROASZero contribution profit after adsFrom the product’s real variable costs
Target ROASThe return that preserves your chosen profit marginFrom BEROAS plus a defined profit goal
Scaling thresholdThe lowest return accepted while budget risesFrom profit, cash flow and data stability

Confusing these levels is expensive. Scaling toward break-even scales revenue without scaling profit. The larger the budget, the faster the gap reaches your bank account.

The break-even ROAS formula

You can apply this formula directly with the BEROAS calculator: break-even ROAS = 1 ÷ contribution margin.

The division is easy. The hard part is building an honest margin that includes every cost caused by the order.

Step 1: calculate your contribution margin

Contribution margin = (selling price − variable costs) ÷ selling price.

Variable costs appear because a sale happened: product cost, fulfilment, shipping, payment fees, expected refunds and any usage-based tool cost. Fixed subscriptions stay out of the per-order formula unless you deliberately allocate them for a separate fully loaded view.

Sell at $100 with $60 of variable costs and your contribution margin is 40%.

Step 2: divide one by that margin

Dividing one by a 40% margin gives 2.5x. Each advertising dollar must generate $2.50 in revenue before the order breaks even on variable costs and ads.

Why reported ROAS can mislead you

Ad platforms report attributed revenue. They do not always reflect every refund, dispute or fee that removes money later.

A campaign shows $10,000 in revenue on $4,000 of ad spend, or 2.5x. Subtract $600 in refunds, $500 in chargebacks and $75 in dispute fees. The adjusted amount used in this operating ratio is $8,825, producing 2.21x.

Operating ad-spend ratio = (revenue − refunds − chargebacks − dispute fees) ÷ ad spend.

That gap can turn a comfortable campaign into a marginal one. Reconcile the advertising report with store and payment data on a consistent attribution window.

Factors that move your break-even ROAS

The floor moves whenever the economics of an order move. Track these inputs by product and market:

  • Supplier price and handling charged per order
  • Shipping zones and carrier surcharges
  • Refund, return and dispute rates
  • Average order value from bundles and upsells
  • Payment method, plan and usage-based tool fees

Review them regularly and after any material supplier, price, shipping or refund change. An old floor creates false confidence.

What to do when ROAS sits below break-even

Lever 1: raise average order value

To raise your average order value (AOV), bundle a $25 phone case with a $15 screen protector that costs $2.50. If the same payment and platform rates apply, the new $40 offer carries about $9.50 in variable costs, a 76.26% contribution margin and a 1.31x break-even ROAS. At the same 3.5x ROAS, estimated contribution after ads rises from $11.60 to about $19.08.

Lever 2: cut variable product costs

In the $100 example, reducing COGS from $15 to $10 drops total variable costs to $22.10. Margin rises to 77.9% and break-even ROAS falls to 1.28x. Ask for tiered quotes and compare like-for-like landed costs before committing volume.

Lever 3: stop or redesign a structurally weak offer

Set a maximum acquisition cost from contribution profit before launch. If enough spend and conversion data show that the offer cannot acquire orders below that ceiling, diagnose price, page, creative and traffic quality. Stop when the economics remain negative after the planned tests. More spend does not repair a margin problem.

The faster alternative can be a product with more room between landed cost and market price. Copyfy helps you compare active products, ads and competing stores, but those signals still need validation against your own costs.

Frequently asked questions

What is a good ROAS for dropshipping?

There is no universal good ROAS. Start with the product’s break-even ROAS, then calculate the higher target that preserves the contribution profit your business needs.

How often should I recalculate break-even ROAS?

Review it regularly and whenever price, supplier cost, shipping, payment fees or refund behavior changes materially.

Can products have different break-even ROAS values?

Yes. Each product and bundle has its own cost structure. One blended catalog target can hide products that lose money.

Does break-even ROAS include refunds?

Only if you include an expected refund allowance in variable costs or calculate ROAS from revenue net of actual refunds. Use one method consistently.

What is the difference between ROAS and ROI?

ROAS compares revenue with ad spend. ROI compares profit with total investment. One evaluates advertising efficiency, the other the economics of the business.

Should I count my time?

Not in the basic per-order floor. Treat owner time and salaries as overhead, then ensure the target ROAS leaves enough contribution to cover them.

Is CPA the same metric?

No. CPA is the acquisition cost in currency. Your break-even CPA equals the contribution dollars available before ads, $72.90 in the $100 example.

Can I use one floor across Meta and TikTok?

The cost-based floor is channel-independent. Attribution and performance differ by channel, so compare both against the same economic definition and revenue window.

Run the numbers before your next campaign

Calculate the floor before launch and place it beside every campaign report. Compare ad sets only after the data is meaningful for your conversion volume and attribution window.

Then choose products and offers with enough margin to make the target attainable. Copyfy can shorten the research by showing active products, ads and competing stores before you commit budget.

Keep the floor visible, but manage toward profit. Break-even tells you when losses stop; your target ROAS tells you whether the business can fund its next move.

What are the features of Dropship.io?

The platform groups about ten tools around three jobs: product research, ad intelligence and competitor tracking. Each feature targets one step of the dropshipping workflow. Here is what each feature does and where it falls short.

Product Library: product discovery

Each product page shows revenue, sale volume and price history. Filters cover price, revenue, variants and shop size, so filtering a niche takes seconds. Keyword filtering also lets you exclude words, on top of advanced filters.

Magic AI Search completes the tool: upload a product photo and it finds similar product listings and active ads. Type a plain-language idea and the AI picks the most relevant item.

The limit: marketplace data says nothing about how the same product will perform on a Shopify store.

Ad Library: ad intelligence and spy

The Ad Library feature gives access to millions of Facebook ads with estimated spend and reach. Filter by creative type, country, language or call to action to spot a trend before it peaks and track performance trends.

One thing to know: reach data covers the European Union only, since Meta publishes it only for the EU. A strong ad in the US can look modest in the tool.

The Advertiser Tracker alerts you when a brand launches a burst of new ad creative, often a sign it is about to scale. That ad intelligence is helpful to identify trends early.

Competitor tracking: Competitor Research and Sales Tracker

The Competitor Research tool lists every store selling the same product as you, with each app it runs and its sale estimates, for a complete view of the competition. It will save a lot of time compared with manual Google searches.

The Sales Tracker tool follows shops and products daily, with estimated sales and revenue. A creator database finds creators who drive sales, helpful if you need UGC creative or affiliates.

Portfolio: the weekly product drop

Every Monday at 12 PM EST, the Portfolio delivers a product drop of up to 40 items picked by the Dropship.io team. Each drop lands in your portfolio and includes:

  • an AliExpress and Alibaba supplier link with supplier cost
  • a saturation level and a competition score
  • a margin breakdown per sale
  • ad interest ideas for your marketing

You import a product in one click to Shopify (title, images, description, price, variants) or to AutoDS. The tool does not handle shipping or fulfillment: AutoDS covers that side of the automation.

Each free resource completes the platform: an AI store builder, a Chrome extension that works like a companion app, a theme detector and CPA, ROAS and BEROAS calculators. Dropship University adds a series of dropshipping course videos, the most useful free resource for a beginner.

Is Dropship.io data accurate?

Dropship.io data is estimated. The pricing page itself describes the TikTok Shops Tracker figures as estimated sales. No third-party tool can access the Shopify admin of a competitor store.

WinningHunter, a direct competitor, gives database accuracy a 5/10. Accuracy depends on the source:

  • TikTok Shop: sale counts are public, so estimates stay close to reality
  • Shopify stores: revenue rebuilt from public signals, rougher
  • Ad spend: ranges calculated by Meta for the EU

Use the data to compare, never to predict. A product showing three times the sales of another deserves a closer look. A store showing $80,000 in revenue guarantees nothing. In one test on a real store, the figures shown didn’t match its actual sales: run the same test on yours if you have one.

A best seller is a product that sells every single week. Not a lucky break. Your competitor has funded the testing for you. Your job: turn that marketing data into a better strategy and a competitive edge in your market.

In brick-and-mortar retail, stores put their stars on the end-cap displays. In e-commerce, competitive spying follows the same logic: retail giant Amazon even publishes its ranking in real time.

Best seller, trending product, winning product: what’s the difference?

TypeWhat defines itLifespan
Best sellerSteady sales volumeSeveral months or years
Trending productSudden spike in searchesA few weeks
Winning productDemand + margin + low saturationVariable

A trending product can blow up in April and vanish by June. A best seller lasts. The winning product you’re looking for combines both: proven demand and a market that’s still open.

The 4 signals a best seller sends about your market

  1. Demand is real. Someone is selling, so someone is buying.
  2. The psychological price point is tested. You see the range that converts.
  3. The marketing angles are visible: promises, visuals, objections handled.
  4. Saturation can be measured. You can count the sites selling the same item.

With these four pieces of information, you decide based on data rather than gut feeling. That’s the foundation of a competitive edge and the first asset of your sales strategy.

Why is cloning a hit product a mistake?

Showing up six months after the first seller with the same page means fighting on price. Your cost per click climbs. Your profit shrinks.

The right move: look for the adjacent niche. A posture corrector sold “for the office” can be repositioned “for gamers” or “for pregnant women”. Same product, new positioning.

Identify your real competitors before analyzing them

To run a useful competitive analysis, first identify 5 to 10 competitors, split into two categories.

Direct and indirect competitors: who should you watch?

Direct competitors sell the same product to the same audience. Indirect competitors meet the same need with a different solution. For a pet hair brush, a brand of vacuums built for dog hair is an indirect competitor.

Spend 80% of your time on direct competitors. Indirect ones mainly give you ideas for angles and positioning.

Where can you find your competitors in under an hour?

Four sources are enough for this competitor research:

  1. Google: search the product name in your customers’ language. Note the sites that show up in the search results and on Google Shopping.
  2. The Facebook Ad Library (Meta Ads Library): search the keyword and note the pages running ads.
  3. Amazon: the Best Sellers ranking by category (home, sports, beauty) is updated every hour.
  4. Social media: TikTok, Instagram and the Facebook groups in your niche.

On Amazon, also check the “Frequently bought together” recommendations. They directly reveal your audience’s buying behavior and the bundles it approves of.

Finally, keep an eye on the US market. It’s often a few months ahead of other markets, including yours. American stores show you what will soon reach shoppers in your own country. If you sell in Europe, neighbouring markets such as Germany or the Netherlands follow a calendar even closer to yours.

Spot your competitors’ best sellers in 15 minutes

By hand, count 3 min per Shopify store. With Copyfy, Shop Analysis displays the flagship products, traffic and active ads of a store in a few seconds.

The manual method: 3 pages to open

  1. The homepage: look for a “Best sellers”, “Top sellers” or “Most popular” section.
  2. The “All products” collection sorted by sales, which gives you the store’s internal ranking.
  3. The product pages: number of reviews, customer photos, low-stock messages.

Decode Shopify’s sort by sales

Add ?sort_by=best-selling to a collection URL, for example yourcompetitor.com/collections/all. Shopify then ranks the catalog by recorded sales, whatever manual order the merchant has set.

The top 5 in this ranking are the store’s stars. It’s the fastest way to see what sells. Be careful, an older product can stay at the top thanks to its history. Always cross-check with freshness.

Two more useful URLs. ?sort_by=created-descending shows the latest additions. /products.json lists the catalog with the publication date of each item. This information is public and lets you date the new products.

Spot best sellers through advertising

Open the Meta Ad Library (Facebook and Instagram) and search the store’s name. Count the active creatives and check their launch date. A product with 15 or more creatives, running for 30 days and growing in number week after week, is almost certainly a best seller.

Why? Nobody funds a losing campaign for a whole month. For ads shown in the European Union, Meta also displays an estimated reach. It’s the public metric closest to real volume.

On TikTok, check the Top Products section of the Creative Center. Also watch organic social media: an item racking up millions of views in UGC almost always ends up in ads.

Reviews can also be imported through customer review apps. Check that the dates make sense: 200 reviews published on the same day is suspicious.

Finally, a store can hide its collection: rely on the ads instead.

Criterion 1: sales consistency

Name: How to scale your Meta Ads campaigns in e-commerce without blowing up your costs
Introduction: Your e-commerce store runs at a 3 ROAS on Meta. You double the budget. Three days later, your cost per purchase is up 40% and  your margin is gone .
Article:
In short:

  • Only scale a campaign that has exited the learning phase with a ROAS above your break-even point.
  • Raise the budget in steps of 15 to 20% every 48 to 72 hours.
  • Steer by marginal CPA: the cost of each added sale matters more than the average.
  • When vertical scaling plateaus, go horizontal: new audiences, new angles, new creatives.
  • Without a properly set up pixel and Conversions API, your ROAS is wrong and so is your scaling.

Your e-commerce store runs at a 3 ROAS on Meta. You double the budget. Three days later, your cost per purchase is up 40% and your margin is gone.

This guide gives you the thresholds, the pacing and every step to scale your business without breaking what works.

How do you know your campaign is ready to scale?

A campaign is ready when three signals are green at the same time. Out of the learning phase, ROAS above break-even, CPA stable over a week. If even one is missing, leave the budget alone.

SignalThreshold to hitWhere to see it
Learning completeAbout 50 optimization events over 7 days“Delivery” column in Ads Manager
Profitable ROASAbove your break-even ROASYour margin calculation + ROAS column
Stability±15% variance over 7 daysDaily breakdown, last 7 days

Signal 1: the learning phase is over

Meta’s algorithm needs about 50 optimization events over a rolling 7 days per ad set. As long as the “Delivery” column shows “Learning”, the numbers move too much to make a call.

Stuck in “Learning limited”? The problem almost always comes from budget. Here’s how to calculate your floor: target CPA × 50 ÷ 7.

With a €30 target CPA, you need about €214 per day to exit learning within a week. Don’t have that budget? Optimize for a more frequent event (add to cart) or consolidate your ad sets instead of spreading them thin.

Signal 2: your ROAS beats your break-even point

ROAS (return on ad spend) equals revenue ÷ ad spend. On its own, it doesn’t tell you whether you’re actually making money. Compare it to your break-even ROAS: 1 ÷ your margin as a percentage.

Take a product sold at €40 that costs you €12 delivered, plus €2 in payment fees. Your unit margin is €26, or 65% of the price. Your break-even point is 1 ÷ 0.65, so 1.54. Also add your fixed costs per order (apps, customer service, team): they push your break-even point up.

Below 1.54, every sale costs you money. At 2.5, you have room to absorb the cost increase that follows any budget increase. Rule of thumb: wait until you’re 30% above break-even before the first step.

Signal 3: a stable CPA over a week

Three good days aren’t enough. Look at the trend in the daily view. Your results should stay within a ±15% range, with frequency under 2 in prospecting and no CPM drift.

A campaign swinging between €18 and €45 per conversion isn’t ready: let it run one more week.

How do you raise the budget without breaking your current campaign?

The basic rule of vertical scaling: +15 to 20% every 48 to 72 hours, only if your cost over the last 3 days stays below your target. Otherwise, you wait.

Why steps? Every increase pushes the algorithm toward people less qualified than your starting audience. Doubling the budget overnight forces it to find them too fast. Your costs blow up before it can adjust.

This 20% rule comes from what experienced media buyers do in practice, not from an official Meta threshold. Meta publishes no numeric threshold: only a “significant edit” to the budget resets learning.

Steps also let you read the effect of each increase. Jump from €100 to €300 in one go and you’ll never know at what level everything fell apart.

This table is an illustrative example, not a client case. Adjust the amounts to your target CPA.

D1€100Campaign out of learning

In two weeks, you triple your budget without any sudden jump. If a step hurts results, stay on it 3 more days before trying again. If the drop persists, go back to the previous step without shutting everything off.

Steer by marginal CPA, not average CPA

This is the most expensive mistake in the scaling phase. The average cost hides what the sales added by your increase actually cost you.

Here’s the marginal CPA formula: (spend B − spend A) ÷ (sales B − sales A). It measures what each extra sale brought in by the new step costs you.

At €100 per day, you get 5 sales: €20 per purchase. At €150, you get 6.5 sales on average: an average CPA of €23.10. Looks fine. Your marginal CPA, though, is €50 ÷ 1.5 sales, or €33.33.

With a €26 unit margin, every added sale loses you money. You’ve hit this audience’s ceiling. Pushing further means buying revenue at a loss.

The case of Advantage+ campaign budget (formerly CBO)

With Advantage+ campaign budget, long known as CBO, you raise the budget at the campaign level. Meta then splits the money across your ad sets based on their results.

Keep 3 to 5 ad sets per CBO campaign. Beyond that, the budget gets fragmented and each ad set struggles to reach its 50 events.

What strategies can you use to scale a Meta campaign?

You have two levers. Vertical scaling increases the budget on what’s already working. Horizontal scaling keeps budgets reasonable but multiplies audiences, creatives, placements or countries.

CriterionVertical scalingHorizontal scaling
ConceptMore budget, same elementsSame budgets, more elements
SpeedFastSlower to build
Main riskRising marginal CPAAudience overlap
When to use itProfitable, stable ad setWhen vertical plateaus
WorkloadLowHigh (new creatives, new tests)

The right method: start with vertical. Switch to horizontal as soon as your marginal CPA exceeds your unit margin.

Broaden your audiences

Broad targeting has become the default starting point with Advantage+ audience. You let the algorithm find buyers from the signals in your creatives and your pixel.

Other levers to test:

  • 1% lookalike audiences, then 1-3% and 3-5%, built on your buyers from the last 180 days
  • New French-speaking countries (Belgium, Switzerland, Canada) if your logistics can keep up
  • New placements (Instagram Reels, Facebook Stories) with a suitable vertical format
  • Interests related to your niche, in a separate ad set

Duplicate a winning ad set

The method: duplicate a profitable ad set into a new campaign with a higher budget. The original keeps running with its history. Only the copy goes back into learning.

The catch: two ad sets on the same audience enter the same auctions. Meta only lets one of your ads in at a time, so your copies hold each other back.

Avoid duplicating the same ad set more than 2 or 3 times.

Use retargeting as a shock absorber

Retargeting brings back people who have already seen your brand. Its job: offset prospecting costs that rise as you scale.

The segments that perform best in e-commerce:

  • 50% and 75% video views, over 30 or 60 days
  • Engagement with your Facebook page or Instagram account over 30, 60 or 180 days
  • Website visitors over 30 days
  • Adds to cart over 7 and 30 days, excluding buyers

Benchmark: 10 to 20% of your total budget on retargeting. Beyond that, you quickly saturate an audience that stays small.

When and how should you launch a new campaign?

Launch a new campaign in only three cases:

  • New audience or new country
  • New objective or new offer, like a Black Friday promo
  • Winning ad set that has hit its marginal CPA ceiling

For everything else, add new ads to an existing campaign. Every new campaign starts from scratch in learning.

Separate your testing and scaling campaigns

The cleanest structure relies on two campaigns:

  • A testing campaign on ad set budgets, with a small daily budget per creative or per angle
  • A scaling campaign on Advantage+ campaign budget, which only receives winning posts

A post moves to scaling when it beats your target 3 days in a row. Kill rule: once you’ve spent 2 times your target CPA with no sale, you stop.

Reuse the winning post’s ID

When you move a winning ad, don’t recreate it. Choose “Use existing post” and paste the post ID.

That way the post keeps its likes, comments and shares: the social proof it has built up follows you.

A post showing 400 positive comments converts better than the same video reposted with 3 likes. Keep a single post per winning creative and reuse that post across all your campaigns.
